roles.heroLead: An Arlington bathroom gets redone about once a generation, so it had better be done right. The part that decides that isn't the tile — it's the bonded membrane behind it. We build the whole assembly, run a 24-hour flood test, photograph it passing, and only then set tile. No shortcuts, because you're not doing this twice.
roles.costH2: How much does tile installation cost in Arlington, WA?
roles.costP1: Expect $14–$26 per square foot installed for tile work in Arlington — that figure carries the tile, setting materials, substrate prep and labor together, with labor by itself starting at $11/sq ft. A tub-shower surround typically prices at $3,200–$6,800, and a complete bathroom — floor, shower and niche — most often finishes between $6,500 and $14,000.
roles.costP2: Here's the part that surprises people: the shape of the tile moves your bill more than the price tag on the box. Small mosaic means hundreds of cuts and grout lines; a big porcelain plank means far fewer. Labor follows the layout, not the invoice.
roles.costNote: Arlington ranges as of August 2026, covering tile, materials and labor. The number that counts is the written one from your free estimate.
roles.layersLead: Seven layers go under and behind good tile. Every failed shower we open up in north Snohomish County is missing one of them — nine times out of ten the membrane, skipped to keep a few hundred dollars in the budget of a job that later costs five figures to tear apart.
roles.whyP1: Shower leaks work quietly. Water slips past the grout, wicks into the substrate, and surfaces a couple of years later as a spongy hallway floor or a brown ring on the ceiling under the bathroom. At that point you're paying for framing, subfloor, drywall and all-new tile.
roles.whyP2: The waterproofing runs about a tenth of what a shower costs. Leaving it out is the priciest shortcut in the whole remodel.
roles.scopeIntro: These are starting numbers — format, substrate condition and layout push them around. The real one gets written on site, free.
roles.cardShower: Pre-sloped base, bonded membrane, flood test; after that the niche, the curb or curbless entry, and tile. You're paying mostly for what disappears behind the wall — as it should be.
roles.cardFloors: Kitchens, baths, entries, mudrooms, basements. We flatten the subfloor first and add an uncoupling membrane wherever movement or radiant heat asks for one.
roles.cardBacksplash: Subway, herringbone, mosaic sheet or slab-look porcelain. We cut clean around outlets, trim the edges, and match grout to your counter rather than the tile carton.
roles.cardHeated: Electric mat over an uncoupling membrane, resistance-checked before and after the tile goes down, wired on its own circuit. Makes sense only while the floor is already open.
roles.cardRepair: Cracked tiles, crumbling grout, corners letting go in the shower. We'll say plainly whether it's fixable or whether the substrate underneath is already gone.
roles.cardDemo: Tile, thinset and backer stripped out, dust held back with plastic and negative air, all of it hauled away. Your driveway stays clear.

roles.faqQ1: How much does tile installation cost in Arlington, WA?
roles.faqA1: Installed tile work in Arlington runs about $14 to $26 per square foot, with tile, setting materials, substrate prep and labor all inside that range; labor on its own begins at $11 for each square foot. A standard tub-shower surround falls between $3,200 and $6,800; a complete bathroom with floor, shower and niche lands at $6,500 to $14,000. Format matters more than the tile's price: mosaic sheets and large-format both take notably more labor per foot than plain 12×12.
roles.faqQ2: How much does it cost to tile a shower in Arlington?
roles.faqA2: For a standard alcove in Arlington, a tiled shower comes in between $3,200 and $6,800 — demolition, the bonded waterproofing system, a pre-sloped pan, the tile setting, a niche and grout all included. Benches, curbless entries, full-height stone and steam setups run higher. The waterproofing itself is only about a tenth of the total, and it's the piece that heads off the failure that costs tens of thousands.
roles.faqQ3: Do you waterproof showers before tiling?
roles.faqA3: Always. A bonded waterproofing system goes behind every shower we tile — not bare cement board with thinset over it. That means a pre-sloped base, a membrane in sheet or liquid form run up the walls, every corner, seam and penetration sealed, and a 24-hour flood test documented with photos before tile goes on. Grout and tile shed water; they don't stop it. The membrane is what protects your framing.
roles.faqQ4: How long does a bathroom tile job take?
roles.faqA4: Four to six working days covers the typical Arlington bathroom. Day one is demolition and dust control; day two builds substrate and waterproofing, with the flood test running 24 hours after it; setting the tile takes a day or two; the last day is grout, silicone and trim. The shower then needs 24 hours of cure before use. A stand-alone floor is usually a one- or two-day job.
roles.faqQ5: Porcelain or ceramic tile — which is better?
roles.faqA5: For anything wet or walked on, porcelain. It's denser than ceramic, takes in under 0.5% water, resists chipping, and its glazed surface shrugs off the iron tint that Arlington well water leaves on softer finishes. Ceramic still earns its keep on walls and backsplashes, where it costs less and the demands are lighter. Our rule: porcelain on every floor and shower floor, ceramic or glass where it only has to look good.
roles.faqQ6: Can you install a heated tile floor?
roles.faqA6: We do. Electric radiant under tile adds roughly $11–$16 per square foot installed, thermostat included. The mat sits over an uncoupling membrane, gets resistance-tested before and after the tile is set, and runs on a dedicated circuit. Do it while the floor is already open — that's when it's affordable — because adding it later means tearing up finished tile.
roles.faqQ7: Do I need to remove the old tile first?
roles.faqA7: Nearly always. Removal and haul-away runs around $3.50 per square foot, and it buys you the only honest look at the subfloor — rot, movement, and how the new height meets the doorways. Going over existing tile can work when the old floor is flat, sound and well bonded, but it lifts the finished height and buries whatever's wrong underneath. We'd rather find problems at demo than after grout.
roles.faqQ8: How much does a kitchen backsplash cost in Arlington?
roles.faqA8: A typical 30 square foot backsplash in Arlington lands between $1,100 and $2,200 installed — with outlet openings cut, edges trimmed and the grout matched to your counter. The top of that range belongs to labor-heavy layouts: mosaic sheets, herringbone, a picture-frame accent behind the range, or slab-look porcelain run to the ceiling. Straight subway sits at the friendly end.
roles.faqQ9: Can you fix cracked tile or regrout instead of replacing?
roles.faqA9: Often. Repair and regrout pricing opens at $8 per square foot, and it's the honest fix when grout is stained or breaking up, a dropped pan cracked a tile or two, or shower corners need old grout cut out and silicone put in. But hollow-sounding tiles, tiles releasing in a pattern, or a wall with give mean the substrate has failed — a repair there only rents you time. We tell you which you've got before any quote.
roles.faqQ10: Which Arlington neighborhoods do you tile?
roles.faqA10: All of Arlington — Downtown and the blocks off Olympic Avenue, Gleneagle, Smokey Point, Kent Prairie, Arlington Heights, Sisco Heights, Trafton, Cicero and Bryant — plus the surrounding country toward Silvana, Island Crossing, Lakewood and Oso. We also tile in Marysville, Stanwood, Granite Falls, Lake Stevens and across north Snohomish County.
roles.faqQ11: What warranty comes with tile installation?
roles.faqA11: Tile installation from OC Flooring carries a 2-year workmanship warranty — double what we give on carpet, because tile problems surface in year two rather than week two. When we install a waterproofing manufacturer's complete assembly, their coverage applies on top of ours. And because the membrane and the flood test are both photographed, you hold proof of what's behind the wall if you ever sell.
